utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to greet everyone, and without wasting any more time I'll give the floor to the first Defence team for 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Idrizovic.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: First I'd like to provide you with some information. This morning the Judges received a new bundle of documents or exhibits. These are Prosecution exhibits that relate to this witness. You have them so that we can follow everything more easily. So you have in the new file, in the new bundle Prosecution exhibits, and in the old one you have my own exhibits, the Defence exhibits. Mr. Idrizovic, you have a pink file in front of you, and let's go through things in order. Let's first have a look at some of the Prosecution exhibits. The first one, and could we please have it on the screen. It's P 01164. P 01164. That's right. Mr. Idrizovic, do you have that before you? It's an order from the Military Police Administration Jablanica. Have you got it in the bundle? Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you something about the signature at the bottom. As far as I can see this is your signature in the middle?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you briefly tell us why your signature is here and how was this document found, and in fact, did you give the Prosecution this document?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's my signature. I signed it. I signed the document when the investigators asked me to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Is this one of the documents that the ABiH, after entering Doljani on the 27th of July, 1993, found in the headquarters in Doljani?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what happened to these documents? When they found them, where did they take the documents?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this has been explained in the Tuta and Stela case. If you want me to repeat it, I will.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What was said there won't help us. Just be brief. A couple of sentences.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not a problem. Some units of the ABiH 44th Brigade took over part of the village of Doljani and also the HVO command. When they did this, all the documents remained there. And the HVO also took over the command of the 44th Corps. So you have the documents I don't have, and I have the documents you don't have. That's the way things worked. When searching the facility -- well, as far as I know, the military police searched the facility.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. But when they took the documents, where did they take the documents, to you or --

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, to the command of the 44th Mountain Brigade, because those brigade units participated in that action.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you then copy these documents, and who did you give the ones that you had found to and who did you give the copies to?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several days after that event, after the situation up there had calmed down, once the conditions had been met, people from the security of the 44th Mountain Brigade examined the documents. They discovered a lot of interesting documents, and they thought that they might be useful at some point in the future. I was in the command where we all were until the 21st of January, and I had a lot of room there. I had fairly good equipment given the wartime conditions, and I had staff members at my disposal. We didn't have any particular tasks apart from providing security for various buildings, so we had time to deal with this. And as a result, most of the documents were photocopied in the staff where I was and that's that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: On that occasion do you know whether stamps and a typewriter and other equipment were found in the HVO headquarters in Doljani?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I didn't see anything of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, please have a look at the bottom of the document and tell me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry, Ms. Nozica. I'm not quite clear what document you are actually talking about. I saw in the transcript 01164. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's the document. Yes. And it's on the screen, we have it in the electronic system, too, dated the 16th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's have a look at the bottom of the document. I can't see the signature of Livaja. Perhaps you can't see it either.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a bad copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: If it's a bad copy, let's have a look at the stamp. What does it say? Does it say the Municipal Staff, and does it say Jablanica beneath that, the Croatian Defence Council, and I'm just reading the stamp now. It says the Municipal Staff at the bottom and it says Jablanica underneath?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We can't see.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's look at the following document that you have in the file, P 00539. It's a report on the work of the military police in Jablanica for the period of the 24th of September till the 1st of October, 1992. You've been shown this document by the Prosecution. Let's have it on the screen. It will be easier to see the stamp then. Let's scroll down a bit. It says commander of the military police, and we have the stamp. Have a look at it. This document is dated the 1st of October, 1992. You also signed it. It's one of the documents that was found; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Have a look at what the stamp says here. Does it say the Main Staff below and then military police?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we see a difference between these two stamps?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And we can see a difference between the dates. I can also show various stamps from this period of time because they would change. Sometimes we had the 4th Corps, and then the 6th Corps, and then there was the Municipal Staff of the TO, and then there was the Defence Staff. So the name changed three times. So in September and in January, well, I can't really say what we had at that time. Perhaps someone who was there could say that the stamp was changed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Idrizovic, all I want to do is to show that the military police of the Main Staff of Jablanica municipality in September 1992 had its own stamp, number 19, and it's called the Main Staff of the military police. Later on in a document that was apparently made on the 16th of January, 1991, the stamp Municipal Staff Jablanica was used. That's all I have to say about that. Let's continue. You have in your file P 02218. It's a report on the work of the assistant commander for SIS, Mijat Tomic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's have a look at the last page of the document. There are only two pages. It's dated the 17th of April, 1993. There's no doubt about that. And on the second page it reads as follows: "After the operation, there was misappropriation of Muslim vehicles and of other goods, and as a result we reinforced the military police at the Sovicka Vrata check-point and issued a specific order to them so that they could prevent such things from occurring."

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's have a look at the next exhibit that the Prosecution showed you, P 02372. This is a decision apparently taken -- well, in fact, we don't know when, but there is a date on it. It's the 13th of May, 1993, at the top of the document. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Apparently it was signed by Marko --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter didn't hear the surname.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We don't know what the month is. Previously we saw a document dated the 17th of April, 1993. This was obviously a document or a decision taken on the 13th of May, 1993. I'd like to remind you of what you said on page 48, line 20, up to page 49, line 2, and then you repeated this on page 49, line 21 and 22, and in fact after these events in April no mobile goods remained in Doljani. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after that period of time everything had been destroyed. I said they probably weren't torching houses. If there were goods in the houses, then they would be destroying them. I said that all the houses, all the stables, all the chicken coops, and all the mosques had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: If you can answer this question do; if not, just say so. Does it seem logical to you that someone would take a decision on the misappropriation of mobile goods or, rather, do you think this is logical or not? This is not your document. You can't comment on it, but just tell me briefly.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this second document should precede the first one, I think, but I don't think this really changes anything. The situation in the field was such as it was. As to whether it was -- as to whether something was set on fire in the house or taken out of the house, that changes nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Have you ever seen a decree on the armed forces of the HZ HB? Did you ever have an opportunity to see that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, no. That was in Grude.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: A decree.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought you meant office, so a decree.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: A decree on the armed forces of the HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you ever hear or see any other documents about the existence of a military police administration in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as those police forces are concerned, well, there was the military police, the civilian. I don't know what the names were anymore. Don't ask me about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You don't like to discuss the military police, but I have to discuss this subject.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me what you know then. Can we assume that the chief of the defence office, Marko Rozic, should have known what the real name of the military police or the military police administration in Mostar was? Can we assume that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he should have known that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry. We're getting into sheer speculation now, Your Honour. It's been going on actually for some time and this certainly is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, you shouldn't speculate in your questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just asking the witness about what he knows. What he doesn't know is not important. Thank you. We can move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please, sir, are you aware of the fact that in the course of 1992 or 1993 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Coric. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have a question I would like to put to the witness, given what he has said on a number of occasions about the military police. My question is as follows: Witness, your animosity towards the military police, does this concern the military police of the ABiH or the military police of the HVO or both police forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, all military police forces and that includes the MUP. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] I'd like to finish this. If it concerns the HVO military police, please tell me why. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, I think they had and should have had an honourable task. I'm speaking in general. I'm not referring to the HVO, to the armija, but they did something else. They operated in a different manner. Unfortunately, today the police force in our country is still a force that provokes and encourages crime. It supports crime either directly or indirectly. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] My question concerned the military police of the HVO. Can you provide us with any reasons for feeling animosity towards the HVO military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I've understood your question. At this point in time there's nothing in particular I'd like to say against the HVO military police. I was talking in general terms. I didn't have any particular examples in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's move on to another subject. Have a look at 2D 00253. And I'd like to inform the Judges that they can find this document among the bundle of documents I provided yesterday. This is a Defence exhibit. You have it before you, and I hope it will appear on the screen. 2D 00253. You can have a look at it now, Mr. Idrizovic. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you have the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you find the hard copy?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Since we have it on the screen, we can move on. Have a look at the last page. Can we have a look at the last page in the B/C/S version. It's page 4. Page 4. The previous page. It says page 4 on the document. That's it. We can see your signature under item 5; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You attended this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And certain conclusions were adopted at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It was held on the 20th of March, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And you signed the document to show that you attended the meeting and accepted the conclusions?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's have a look at 3D -- this is a Defence exhibit, Defence for Praljak. 3D 00556. And I'd like to inform the Judges that they have the document in the file provided today, but we'll also see it on the screen. So 3D 00556. It is an order. You have it before you so you can read it.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It is about the command of the 4th Corps, and I said that unfortunately we would have to talk about the military police again. Let us take a look at the bottom of the order and see who the author of this order is or who issued it. It is the 4th Corps commander, Arif Pasalic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's see what this is about, although I'm sure you remember it.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is an order, and I'm going to read it out for Their Honours' benefit and for the transcript. "Pursuant to an order on the formation of the military police, the battalion of the 4th Corps of the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and with the aim of fully establishing a military police battalion, a company of the military police in Jablanica, I hereby order," not to read it all.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know what rule this is about.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I have to do it for the record. Now, point 2 says -- well, we have to read point 1. "Team of the 4th Corps command of the RBiH army led by the commander for security, Dziho Sevkija [phoen], Sead Brankovic, and the clerk for the military police and command of the military police battalion, Sekic Nosrid [phoen], will organise a military police company in Jablanica -- shall organise a military police company in Jablanica." "The direct organisation of the military police company and ensuring all the conditions necessary for its establishment will be secured by the commander of the staff defence of the RBiH army of Jablanica, Idrizovic Safet." Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So you had some assignments, too, linked to the military police during the war, did you not?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just that one there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us look at point 5. "The commander of the defence staff of the BH army of Jablanica shall regulate by way of written orders that the museum facility should be evacuated within 24 hours by -- that all forces shall leave the building and the museum and that security should be provided by the RBiH army. The museum shall be used as a centre -- training centre for the BiH army." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is the 11th of January, 1993, and it is the museum which will later on be the location for the holding of prisoners of war, right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, did you act upon this order?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. What did you do?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was supposed to provide logistical support; that is to say, to provide security for the area, for people to be put up there, to ensure that they had food, and they were -- received meals together with members of the BH army. There were a number of centres in town preparing food. So that was my task, to provide logistical support. And from point number 1, you can -- of this order, you can see who was placed in charge of establishing the military police in the first place, and it was my job to create the conditions for its functioning. So I was playing the role of host in a way.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But you had to move the military police of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army too. Someone mentioned the Green Berets yesterday. There were soldiers of both sides. There were refugees from Gacko at the time as well. And the facility, in view of its size, was just taken up in part, in -- a small part of it was occupied. So it was supposed to be freed up, not only for the military police battalion, and we're actually doing here -- am I speaking too fast? We're talking about the military police company. So a part of the battalion in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You mean the military police company?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So if you look at the date, this is the 11th of January. I received an order to form a brigade by the 20th of January. So my role there was somebody who was supposed to do that, and it was the time when the 4th Corps -- when attempts were made to establish the 4th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm interested in the military police company now and some other HVO units that were located there. But anyway, your task was to move them out of there?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was Daidza. There was some HVO police members and some Green Berets, those unfortunate Green Berets of ours. It was a mixed composition there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we take a look at another order of yours that you issued the very next day. You were very expedient and issued the order the very next day. The document is the one that you will find after this document that we're looking at now in your binder. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It's an order dated the 12th of January, 1993. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And in that order of the 12th of January, 1993 it says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It would be useful for the record if you could name the document because later it will not be in this form of a bundle.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. Thank you, Your Honour. Just a moment, please. It was put into e-court yesterday, and it is document 263. Can we have a look at document 263 now, please. I apologise for just a moment. If I can take a moment to look.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we're doing this, I've been reluctant to raise this because I didn't want to interrupt counsel, but we seem to be having an increasing problem with getting the bundles from a number of -- from a number of the Defence. Some are very good about it, I must say, and I want to be fair about that. Some are very good to give us the materials, but others are not so consistent. It's very difficult when we're moving as quickly as this to find and work with the documents. And I know the Judges have the same problem. We have -- I have nothing. I have absolutely nothing over here with this witness. The document comes up on our screen as the B/C/S version. It doesn't do us any good, to be perfectly honest. And it would be most helpful -- I think the Chamber's order was that all cross-examination materials would be provided to the Prosecution at the end of examination-in-chief and we would much appreciate that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher just place this document on the ELMO. And with respect to the comment made to the Prosecution, I'd like to say as the Prosecution knows full well, the Defence of Bruno Stojic always provided a hard copy to the Prosecution until we passed on to the system of disclosing them one day before we start our cross-examination. So the Prosecution has been given all the documents that the Defence of Mr. Stojic intends to use. But I will find the number of the document since it was placed in e-court yesterday. It might not be there yet. But the witness has it now. It's on the ELMO. Can we pan down a bit so that we can see the signature on this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Witness, can you take a look at the signature?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have the document. The signature is mine. There's nothing that I challenge about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, is this the 12th of January, 1993, when you issued an order ordering the military police company and the HVO units located in the museum facility to leave the building within a 24-hour deadline so that the building can -- could be used for the purpose it was intended for and that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, this doesn't do. We have a document now in B/C/S on the screen. We do not know what number it has. We still do not know, and we do not have an English translation. I'm sorry, this is not the way it can be done. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. You have the translation in English. Since the witness has found it, could he read out the number?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, might I be of assistance. In e-court for General Praljak the same document is 3D 00554. It's the same document. Both the English and Croatian versions. So perhaps that will be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly request that the English version be placed on the screen so they could read what it says. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the number of the document is?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I see. 264. And I think that that is the document that Their Honours have. 2D 00264. And it was in yesterday's binder. [In English] 266.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. I obviously had the wrong number. 266. Have you found the document, Your Honours? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, we read point 1, did we not? In point 2 it says: "The military police company of Jablanica is to be situated in the armed forces barracks in Jablanica, and all the materiel not assigned is to be returned to the Jablanica defence staff warehouse together with the record on the hand-over." Is that what it says? Was the order complied with?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure that you'll find something unclear here as will Their Honours. Now, when I spoke about animosity towards the military police earlier on, we're now establishing a military police company, and now I'm throwing out a military police company from the museum now.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I don't have much time. Would you refrain from expounding?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Green Berets unit which proclaimed itself to be the military police. It was not within the effective chain of command of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Idrizovic, I'm speaking about the military police as it refers to the HVO units and military police company pursuant to this order, and we can see that you complied with that order. You carried it out.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me, what was the -- or, rather, there was a document previously, and we saw that all this was done in order to create a training centre there for the BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Coric, your time has expired, but go ahead and ask your question quickly. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] I have to intervene. If somebody says that the HVO had a military police company, that is just not true. That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say that. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Counsel said that just now. Look at her last sentence, and she said the military police company in Jablanica HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure I understood what Mr. Coric's comment related to. I'm just reading the document. I'm reading the document and it says under number 1 "The military police company and HVO units."

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it meant our company, the BH army company and the HVO units.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it says in the document, and I base my knowledge exclusively on what it says in these documents. Now, in the previous order issued by Mr. Arif Pasalic, it said that the premises of the museum were earmarked to be a training centre. Did it actually become a training centre ever?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we now look at what we know already, go through what we know already? It became a centre for holding prisoners of war, did it not?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And a centre where civilians were put up as we saw yesterday.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, was there any idea for having this centre, this compound, which included the museum to make it into an Islamic centre?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: May we look at document 1D 01030 now, please. It is a document from the Prlic defence, a very brief conclusion, and we have the translation of it, too, so could you place the two documents on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the number because it is not in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D 01030. It is a document by the Prlic Defence, and Your Honours have it in the Croatian version in your binders which you received today, but you'll be able to see the English version on e-court because the Prlic defence lent us the document yesterday. So 1D 01030 is the document number. 1D 01030.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, the 1D 01030 is not on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although I received information that it was already in e-court, obviously it is not, so may we have the document placed on the overhead projector, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, may we have the calculations for the time used, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue? I'll get through the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We can see that it is the 14th of September, 1993. Can we see the signature. Pan down for the signature, please. This is a document which is the municipality of Jablanica, signed by Mr. Cibo, right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It is the 14th of September, 1993. That is the date of the document. And the president, Safet Cibo, brings in the following conclusions: He grants permission or gives agreement for the initiative launched to build an Islamic centre on the free space of the memorial complex called the battle on the river Neretva in Jablanica, which includes the mosque, the shops, the children's nursery, the cemetery, and other facilities. Point number II speaks about the plans and projects for the area. And the conclusion comes into force on the day it was issued; that's what point III says. Now, Mr. Cibo was president of the Assembly at that time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Nozica, I would be interested to learn how this is related to our case. I must confess that I fail to follow the thread that you probably spun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I wanted to add this, Counsel Nozica: We've spent 30 minutes, exactly 30 minutes for the witness to confirm that he had a certain responsibility vis-a-vis the museum, that they placed detainees there, and that now there was this project for the museum. Now, how is that relevant and useful for our case with regard to Articles 73, et cetera, regarding Sovici, Doljani, and the HVO actions? What do you wish to prove? What is your case here? Ask him your questions -- everything you've been doing for the past 30 minutes was not useful, because I do not see what I can use with respect to a judgement on the basis of what you've put forward in your 30 minutes. It is not a trial of either the witness or the BiH -- ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, on a number of occasions the witness said that if we bear in mind the relevant period, the relationship between the HVO and the ABiH up until the time the conflict broke out was correct, and documents that concern transfer of the military police obviously show that the intention wasn't to do what the armija had written in the order. The intention was to expel or to transfer units from that centre, units of the HVO and the ABiH, and that shows that the relationship between the HVO and the ABiH wasn't correct as the witness has said, in fact. As far as my questions and the paragraphs of the indictment are concerned, my questions remained within the framework, within the scope of the Prosecution's questions to the witness. And there was much about the relationship between the HVO and the ABiH throughout 1993 up until the 17th of April, 1993. If these answers don't assist the Chamber, I regret that, but I hoped that his answers would show what the relationship was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Put a brief question summarising everything that you want to demonstrate. Put a question to the witness and he'll answer the question. Would you like to ask the witness whether the ABiH and the HVO were on very good terms up until a certain date, and after that date this relationship deteriorated? If you do that, that would be useful, but it's not necessary to pass 30 minutes in order to arrive at such a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that suggestion, Your Honours. On the basis of the witness's answers during the last 10 minutes, that's how much we've spent on this subject matter. On the basis of his answers, I came to the understanding that the HVO and the ABiH units were transferred from these facilities but not for the reasons stated in the order. How this could have affected and whether it could have affected the relationship between the HVO and the ABiH, well, we will come to that ourselves or with the help of the following witness. I believe that the question that I might put to the witness, if I asked whether the relationship deteriorated after their activities, well, I'm afraid that his answer wouldn't help Mr. Stojic's defence or the -- or the Chamber, because I don't believe the answer would correspond to the documents we have seen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Answer what counsel has just said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I regret the fact that Ms. Nozica came to the -- came to a completely erroneous conclusion. I carried out the order of my superior, and I had to make a great effort. He had more problems with the HVO than with the company of military police that was, to a large extent, outside of the chain of command. The reason for which in mid-January, and these people were moved from the centre, well, the reason for -- is that -- in fact, this was never done. So all these activities were in vain. I think the HVO units and the municipality didn't have great problems when it came to securing premises. Those who were in Jablanica in the course of the war know that they had this premises in a construction company. They know that the HVO headquarters were a hundred metres away from the command I was in. There was the military police company that did enter this building on one occasion without any authorisation, but later I think that this problem was solved. So as far as the town is concerned, there were no problems. After the war we found this out: One of the reasons which Safet Cibo came to Jablanica was that we allowed the formation of parallel authorities in Jablanica. I have the documents, but this isn't what we're dealing with here today in this case. We had Cibo because of good term -- because of the good relationship with the HVO. If Ms. Nozica returns to Bosnia and wants to have a look at the documents about this, she can. I think I'm right when I say what I'm saying, but naturally this is isn't what we're discussing now. We had problems because we acted in a correct way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we've heard Mr. Stojic's version, your version, and the Judges will determine and assess what is true and what is not. For the next Defence team, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Idrizovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have a lot of documents here for 30 minutes, so try and be brief.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the bundle of documents for the Praljak Defence there are lots of documents that have already been used. This was prepared after -- immediately after the examination-in-chief. I won't be going through all the documents. I'll go through the documents that have not yet been referred to with the exception of one document. So we'll be taking up 20 minutes, and General Praljak will take the floor for 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Mr. Idrizovic, as you can see, we are a little short of time. Could we see P 00708. Could this be shown to the witness. It's 3D 00290 in the bundle. P 00708 is in the Prosecution file that was provided before the examination of this witness. It's an order dated the 6th of November, 1992. Could we have a look on the second page. You can't see it right now. Have you got a hard copy? We can provide the witness with a hard copy. It was signed by General Praljak. It was about establishing check-points. You can see what it's about.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And the document also relates to what you said in the course of the examination-in-chief. You said that in November you would meet General Praljak. He would come to Jablanica, and he then promised to calm the situation down. You were asked whether you knew what the results of his activities were, whether General Praljak did what he promised to do. So now that you see this document, this order, does the order show that what was said would be done was actually done; namely, that they would work together, there would be mixed check-points or jointly-held check-points, joint patrols. You understand what I'm saying. Do you agree that they started implementing these things?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some things were carried out. There were these joint patrols, jointly held check-points, et cetera. Sometimes this took a little longer. Sometimes it went faster. Sometimes orders weren't carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: But they did exist?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have much time. We have to hurry. Have a look at General Praljak's signature. Next to the signature you can see a stamp?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And can you see that the stamp is a joint stamp or, rather, it's a stamp of the ABiH and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But we never received any information about the existence of such a staff. Had we seen -- we never saw such a stamp. I'm not saying this document isn't correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: In Jablanica you weren't informed about this?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Could we see P 002 -- P 00727. And this also concerns joint action. The 10th of November, 1992 is the date. P 00727 is the number. It's on appointing temporary members of the command. Again, it's been signed by General Praljak, and it's a joint stamp again. You know who Ante Prkacin was?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: He was the Chief of Staff in the HVO, and Arif Pasalic represented the ABiH. Thank you. Let's have a look at the next document. P 00795. If you could show this to the witness because I don't think it's in the binder. It's a Prosecution exhibit. Mr. Idrizovic, you know who Zdravko Sagolj is. We've heard about him. He was the commander of the Herceg Stjepan Brigade. In Konjic on the 24th of November, 1992, Zdravko Sagolj appointed two individuals, Ivica Tomic and Soldo Berislav. Did you know Soldo Berislav?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He works in the MUP in Jablanica now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes. He was appointed to a joint commission, so this had to do with establishing joint check-points, joint patrols, and as a result two individuals were appointed, and on this basis of parity, and this is something we can also see in the first order, one policeman who was appointed from the HVO and three HVO members. They were appointed to these -- this joint commission. Did you receive this document?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could the witness please be shown 3D 00561. Let's immediately go to page 3D 20/0072. And for the Bench, the page is 3D 20-0090, or in the upper right corner L0068585. These are minutes from the meeting held in the office of the -- of President Tudjman on the 27th of March, 1993, upon the return of the delegation of Alija Izetbegovic and Mate Boban from New York.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Pinter, I quite understand the difficulties the Defence has to identify and put into order and label the documents and so forth, but we also should be able to find them. This document again I have not found. There is no number that has a slash in it. You gave a number 3D 20/0072. This is not an element of our numbering, and I do not manage to find this document. I didn't manage to find the previous one either.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter apologises the Defence counsel said hyphen, or dash, not a slash.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, Hyphen or slash or whatever. The numbers run through, and I do not find it here. 3D 00 ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D00561. To assist the Bench to fine the page, I also said the number at the bottom of the page or in the right upper corner. It would help you to find the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the number at the bottom of the page is the B/C/S number, and perhaps the English version doesn't correspond to 3D72.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, I said that the page was 3D20-0090. I emphasised that and I said in the upper right-hand corner it says L0068585. That's the number. That's the number of the translation. Could we have this on the screen perhaps. I'd like to move on so as not to waste more time. 3D20-0090. That's the number at the bottom in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Have you had the opportunity of looking at the document now?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: In fairness, you must know what we have, of course, and we have this thick bundle, and in the beginning of the bundle there's a list of the documents it's supposed to contain. My file stops at 3D 00559. So no wonder I cannot find 561, because the bundle ends before that. Is there another bundle maybe somewhere in this sea or avalanche of paper that we are in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to point this problem out to all Defence teams. When you prepare your file for your cross-examination, do so so that the questions that you put are followed by the documents so that we can go to the first document, the second, the third, the fourth, as you put your questions. But if we have to first go to the back of the bundle then to the middle and to the beginning, we get lost. I know it's very complicated, but you have the means. So prepare your files and follow a certain order so that we can start with the first document and continue to the last. Otherwise, things will be very complicated. This also concerns the Prosecution, because the Prosecution has very good files, but they don't go through them in order, and this means that the Judges have to try and find the relevant documents. It would be a lot simpler if we followed a certain order. Mr. Karnavas, for example, has his files prepared, and he has them in a certain order. He goes through that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Pinter, in fact you may have proceeded the way the President suggests. I now find 3D 00561, and while in the list it is at the end, it is in the beginning in the file, and I have found it now. But it took some time, as you can see, and it's not very economical if we have to do this, and it's not futile for us to see it. So please do not take this as formalism. It's a real problem. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't want to belabour this now, Your Honour, but in defence of both some of the Defence teams and the Prosecution, the reason they're put in the order that they're in, frankly, we've actively considered the various options and have opted to date to keep them in numerical order for this reason. A numerical order is an order that can remain the same for all purposes. Once you start shifting them around and if the order changes for some reason, then it does become very difficult because there is no rhyme or reason to it. And, quite frankly, Your Honours, some of the bundles are put together two weeks before the witness comes when the exhibits are sent out, then there's the proofing, there's decisions made not to use documents, the order of documents changes, and if we have to re-order them every time it changes, frankly some of that would be done on the morning of court. And I realise the problems it creates, as we can all see, but we have come to the option, decision or practice that if we at least keep them in the numerical order, that order will never change and everyone can find it at least by that system. I do apologise that it's sometimes not the best, but it does seem to be the best general approach to it. I must say we do appreciate the assistance that we generally get from the Praljak Defence team, and they're usually very good about providing the bundles of the documents. It is difficult when we're moving this quickly, I think, for everyone in the courtroom, including the Judges and the Prosecution, frankly to keep up with finding the documents. Especially when the counsel and the witness are speaking the same language, we find that by the time we find the document the questions and the answers -- we're already behind the question and answer, and that's also part of the problem. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: While we're talking about this, the Prosecution, of courses has the luxurious way of numbering the documents which makes it much easy to handle it, because here now and then, as you must have experienced, suddenly a number just falls off. That doesn't assist either. But I agree that it is of course much more work to do it the way the Prosecution does. I just say this as a suggestion. And I would -- personally I would also agree that the numerical system is probably the soundest one because this is something one can always go by and one knows that five comes under four -- after four. Usually.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to just give one explanation, and I thank the Prosecutor for prompting me there. The preparation of the Defence documents was conducted on Tuesday, when the examination-in-chief was completed, and according to guidelines from the Bench, from the Trial Chamber, we were supposed to send in the list of documents that we're going to present and tender immediately after that. But I didn't know which other documents would be tendered from the other Defence teams, which is why there is so many documents in the file. But I'd now like to move on and discuss this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Mr. Idrizovic, this is a speech by Alija Izetbegovic, and he was interrupted by asking that Konjic be solved first, and Alija Izetbegovic says, "But we'll solve that in Konjic." So that is the 27th of March when the conflicts were already under way. And then Gojko Susak takes the floor, and you know of course who Gojko Susak was, and he says Alija --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down. It's impossible to translate at this speed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: -- Praljak. Nobody can accuse me of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You are much too fast. The translation doesn't follow. This is -- it's like when you have to give a speech somewhere they tell you you have 45 minutes and some speakers then think they double the speed to say all they want to say and it -- it invariably fails. It is just like this. It doesn't work.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but you have the translated document in front of you and I have to get through this with the witness. I only have 20 minutes at my disposal, and I have a lot of areas which I wish to deal with which I think are very important as far as the Defence is concerned, and that is why I'm hurrying through this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, have you had a chance of reading through what Gojko Susak says?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Do you know who Jasmin Jaganjac is?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Do you know what Jasmin Jaganjac was on the 27th of March, 1993? Do you know that --

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Did you hear that he was an advisor to President Izetbegovic, a military advisor?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was with Mr. Izetbegovic and Jaganjac on the 1st of January, 1993, in Mostar and then he was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And that was later on. That's March?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's another paradox, that the general of one country can be the military advisor of the president of another country. That can be a paradox, but it might also be an attempt to do something jointly, pooling efforts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now would you take a look at the next page, please where the -- where President Tudjman is speaking and he is says the following: "Alija, I want to tell you something now. I agreed that General Praljak should go to Herceg-Bosna or Bosnia-Herzegovina after I had statements from him that he thinks that nonetheless our Croats over there are perhaps doing something wrong vis-a-vis the Muslims, that their conduct towards them is wrong perhaps." And then the president goes on to say: "So understand me, when somebody like that says things like that, you know that that is so. And because of that I'm in favour of you giving a joint statement down there for the benefit of both sides." Mr. Idrizovic, can we conclude from this that General Praljak in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina was there with the aim of calming the situation down over there and to try and ease tensions?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I think that's just going too far.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please for the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: To ask this witness to voice that kind of a broad opinion on the role of Mr. Praljak on several years of armed conflict I just think that's too broad to ask this witness to give an opinion like that. I -- if she wants to ask questions about this particular document and what was said, of course. But this opinion is too broad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well. But the question could perhaps be summarised and have the same goal this way: Witness, you have heard the Defence and they're talking about a meeting between Mr. Izetbegovic and other individuals, and what was the result of that meeting on the basis of what we have here is that General Praljak is going to go in situ because there is some behaviour on the part of the Croats which isn't perhaps the right one. Now, the -- the -- under these conditions it seems that General Praljak will go in the field. You were there yourself. You saw General Praljak. Now, did you have the feeling that when General Praljak arrived it was to try and deal with the problems that were occurring there concerning the conduct of Croats and their behaviour toward Muslims? Was that your impression? Do you agree with the text here or not? What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in principle I can say that every meeting, every time people met to discuss something was in order to reach an agreement of some kind, and Mr. Praljak and everybody else, when they came, always had meetings in order to calm the situation down. That was the declarative part, the declarations that were made, if I can put it that way. However, in practice you couldn't feel that a lot was done to change the situation. And I said previously that when orders were received about joint check-points and joint patrols, for example, that would last a very short period of time or not at all or a longer period of time, but there was no continuity in this process. There was not much progress. You would take one step forward after agreements like that and then two steps back, and that was the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So your answer is and you've already given us the answer the previous day. That's your answer. Now, what we as Judges are interested in is this: Why, for what reason was this difference between the orders and declarations made, declarations of intention and principle, and how they were executed and implemented on the ground. Why was there no agreement between and conformity between what was decided and what was done. So if it was decided that General Praljak was to be sent there to try and calm the situation down, why didn't relations in fact calm down between the two communities? Have you got an explanation to give us? Why wasn't it followed through? So that's a very precise question. This is an example of how to ask a very precise question, and this is food for thought for the Defence to follow suit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to answer? Can I answer now? Do you want me to answer? Yes. Well, there are two things involved here. First of all, the lower-down commanders perhaps did not -- were not efficient in carrying out the orders from their superiors or that the agreements reached were not really sincere, that the participants were not sincere in reaching agreements and that they were trying to trick each other. There's no third explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now, to continue on from that answer of yours, I'd like us to see the next document, and it is P 02059, and at the same time P 02 -- P 02078. It is a joint declaration which my colleague Ms. Alaburic used with the following number: P 02088. So I'm going to use the number used by Ms. Alaburic, but I gave you the two numbers that are in my file. Mr. Idrizovic, as you can see, this is a joint declaration, and yesterday with Ms. Alaburic you discussed it. You spoke about this joint statement between Alija Izetbegovic and Mate Boban which was given on the 24th of April, 1993. And with respect to the agreement reached on the 3rd of March, 1993, in New York. Do you have the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean 59?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: P 02078. It is a joint statement by Alija Izetbegovic and Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: You've found it?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now, with -- you discussed this with Ms. Alaburic. It is agreement reached on the 3rd of March, 1993, almost a month and a half before the joint statement came. And would you pay attention to page 2.4, because in .4 it says what the points of the agreement were on the 3rd of March, 1993, between Alija Izetbegovic and Mate Boban in New York. They agreed and decided that the conflicts between the HVO and the BH army were contrary to the policy waged by the representatives of those two ethnic groups and that any further continuation of the conflict would seriously endanger the realisation of their political goals, that is to say, independence, autonomy and territorial integrity for the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina within the frameworks of the Vance-Owen Plan, which the signatories accepted and signed, as well as the success in the struggle against the aggressor who wanted to break up the state. Now, this agreement signed on the 3rd of March, 1993, the public was informed about this only on the 24th of April, 1993. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I didn't know about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have a problem with the date, because in my document the date at the end is April 25. On the last page of the English version. Right under the signatures.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour. However, in the preamble, in the preamble of this joint statement Mr. Alija Izetbegovic and Mr. Mate Boban it says at a meeting which they -- which was convened in Zagreb on the 24th of April, 1993. The presiding people were the representatives of the international conference of Yugoslavia and ended in 00 -- at 0045 hours. That is why the date is the 25th of April, because 45 minutes after midnight was when the statement was actually signed, but the event took place on the 24th of April in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And refers back to the 3rd of March --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In point 1 it refers back to the 3rd of March when the agreement was reached. The witness has just told us that he didn't know about this. You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: You didn't know, Witness, that the agreement was reached on the 3rd of March?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all contacts during this period - that is to say, right before the conflict erupted - the Croatian side always said, always spoke about this agreement, that it had been signed. We were a little taken aback because nobody provided us with any explanation. Now, don't hold me to the dates, but a little after this, and I have the exact date in some of my papers, we did ask Mr. Izetbegovic when we did have occasion to meet him, and he said that he had not signed the Vance-Owen Plan, and -- and it was about the cantonisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, of course, that that plan was never signed, was not signed. So, yes, it was discussed; but, no, it was not signed, which means that it did not have the force of law.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: That's how Mr. Izetbegovic explained it to you, is it?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: But now you can see the signature is there?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm telling you what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: May we now have the next document shown to the witness and it is 3D 00547.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And before that I'd like to ask how much more time I have because I have to leave some time for General Praljak's questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, would you do the calculations, please. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: While that's being done, Your Honour, just to correct the record, I don't think there's any evidence that this document indicates a signature or a signing by Izetbegovic of the Vance-Owen Plan. These are preliminary documents apparently about some documents signed on the 3rd of March. I'm not quite sure, but I think it's a mischaracterisation to use this document to say that Izetbegovic had signed the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have four more minutes. You've used up 16 minutes, so that leaves four. And we'll -- we'll -- if Mr. Praljak wishes to use 10 minutes, he can do so and we'll listen to him with great interest. So four minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just deduct Mr. Scott's intervention from those four minutes, please, because this is a specific concrete document and his arguments should be raised in some other -- on some other occasion. But that is why I would like to refer to another document, P 02059, because it is the minutes from the presidential offices from which we can see in detail everything that went on, how it happened and what the result of the joint statement was. That is given at the end. That is why those two documents go together and I'd like to look at them together. They are in fact one document. This statement is the result of the negotiations and talks held on the 24th of March -- April, I am sorry, April. Now, I'd like to present and tender one more document and then I'll hand the floor over to General Praljak for his questions. The document is 3D 00547. And it is while we're waiting for the document on e-court, Sefer Halilovic issuing an order on the 29th of January, 1993. Perhaps we can provide the witness with a hard copy not to waste time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this document? Have you ever seen it before?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday or the day before, when we were discussing the arrival of Mr. Cibo down there, that we had some documents -- or, rather, that we came into possession of this document only after the war. We didn't know why Mr. Cibo was coming. At least where we were in Jablanica there was no reason for anybody to come down there, because the authorities were functioning. Actually, there were two authorities functioning at that time. There were no conflicts, and then somebody came to stir the murky water. Now, my team and I, working on the chronology that I mentioned at the beginning when I talked to the Prosecutor, I think, I said that part of the documents which -- that we came into possession of them only after the war. So this was probably found in the 4th Corps when it was captured. We did not have this document. It was correspondence between the Supreme Command Staff and the corps command staff. Of course we didn't have this kind of document but they sort of --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: You were in a quandary about them. Would you agree with me that as far as Jablanica is concerned and the relationship between the HVO and BH army that the situation would not have developed in the way it did had this not happened, had not the presidents in the Konjic municipality being replaced and that Cibo arrived. He was supposed -- who stirred up the relations there.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me to speculate. What would it have been had it been.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've already answered that. I answered that before.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The witness said that he had already answered that and it's my fault for not letting you finish. Would you repeat your answer? My question was: The radicalisation of relations and -- ensued after the arrival of Dr. Cibo between the HVO and BH army.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only that. The overall situation in the field took a negative turn. I'm not only thinking of the Jablanica municipality here, but generally speaking the situation deteriorated around Konjic and in Konjic especially. The situation around Mostar too. We had already been cut off from Mostar, and we had nothing to do with Mostar, nothing at all, no physical links, no technical links, and the situation was very difficult for us in the military sense. I'm not speaking about the political sense. I'm speaking militarily. The situation was very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The agreement was signed on the 3rd of March, 1993, was it not, and you knew nothing about that. Had you known about that, perhaps the situation would have been different.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the agreement had been signed and if it came into force, I must have -- I would have had to know about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Well, you can see it from this document. But that completes my questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give the floor to Mr. Praljak now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you have 10 minutes. I know that you're not going to speed up, I hope. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] If I could be given a little more time for this witness and not -- and I won't ask the following witness anything.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, the witness is saying, and I'll repeat his words, that Safet Cibo arrived because we had good cooperation with the HVO. That's what he said. That's what the witness said, and that's what it says in the transcript. Isn't that right, Mr. Idrizovic?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't put it quite that way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: We'll read through the transcript.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the transcript says, but I know what I said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let's go back to the beginning after the conflict in Prozor I had three meetings in Jablanica at various periods of time. That was immediately after the conflict. I had one meeting; there were about a hundred, 120 people there, and you were there too. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: The situation wasn't easy?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: We managed to discuss things in a normal human way, political way; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And because of that conflict I was insulted in various ways with justification and without justification; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is it correct to say as some witnesses have said that after that conflict we won't go into the reasons for the conflict but after that conflict by the end of the year, well, the situation was relatively calm throughout the entire area, from Travnik, Jablanica, Konjic, and Mostar. For about two months was there relative calm in that area?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So it was calm. After the conflict in Gornji Vakuf was the situation relatively calm in Konjic, Jablanica, Mostar? Did people work together and so on?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct too. But the relationship developed in a certain way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I understand you, Mr. Idrizovic, because that's correct. The situation became calm. There was no political solution. As a man, you felt increasingly helpless; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You felt that people were becoming more and more radical; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You felt that your influence was diminishing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You -- that made you increasingly unhappy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally. You probably felt like that too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: That's what we're speaking about. Judge Antonetti put a fundamental question to you. How is it that given all the efforts made at various levels each following period meant that the situation had deteriorated and had become even more unstable and minor problems would provoke serious consequences; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But you had a higher level of responsibility than I did, and you had a better overview of the situation. You had better communication with everyone else. I can only speak in local terms.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I have very little time. You also said that the war had had elements of aggression within it.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Would you agree that the -- the JNA and the Serbian units launched the aggression?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And then it turned into a civil war. There were elements of a civil war. We know what that means. People who were not under control, the political scene became more and more radical; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And then there were elements of a religious war, especially when the Mujahedin arrived, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not only that. But we can talk about the Mujahedin, if you like. When I mentioned a religious war, I said that in a negative context. All three confessions in Bosnia-Herzegovina were in a negative context. I think they contributed to the war to a large extent, and no one here will discuss that matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'd like to discuss that matter because you're a political scientist too. But let me tell you the following -- or ask you the following: Was there a muderis brigade in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well, in Konjic. But muderis also had a line-up in Jablanica on one occasion in 1994?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was called the 4th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Is muderis an official from the Islamic community?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So that's some sort of an official?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Was the thought of that brigade as follows, was the ideology of the brigade as follows: I've shown this to the Judges during my opening speech: Did they cry out, Who are we fighting for? And did they say for Allah?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And who were they fighting against?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We're, once again, back into talking about Mujahedin and everything else on the other side and tu quoque, and we always get into this with Mr. Praljak. It's not relevant to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak is talking about a 4th Muslim Brigade. I've just found out about that. And apparently elements of this 4th Brigade were also present in Jablanica. Mr. Praljak seems to be saying, and you can deny this if you like. You never saw them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did see them, but they didn't stay in Jablanica. Perhaps they came on one occasion to the stadium or to the area near the museum. I don't know where exactly. And there was a review perhaps, but this was more for propaganda purposes. I think that was at that time and normal people didn't like that either. When they were crying out wasn't normal. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: But they would say who are we fighting for, for Allah. Against whom? The Wallachs. The Wallachs are the Christians; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But you must admit that they had about 500 units and the 4th Corps had far more, about 20.000. So this didn't represent much of a force.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So I'm talking about elements, not about anything else. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] And as far as what Mr. Scott said, your analysis that you're trying to carry out here by separating what the witness has said, when he talked about the elements of civil law and the way everything was linked up, when you say that all this is tu quoque, well, this is not a possible position. We're dealing with a -- the people, with the control, with Praljak, Petkovic, and Prlic could have had. That's the substance of this indictment, and you can't separate certain matters from each other. This is no justification. But I'm following the same logic that you're following. According to that logic, according to your logic, 500 American officers in Iraq would have to go to prison immediately because they can't control everything, and I totally reject this point of view. I'm not justifying any crimes. I want to determine what my role is here when it comes to preventing such crimes or provoking such crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I will tell you what your role is. It is to ask questions and not start arguing with the Prosecution. You are using your time for a wrong purpose. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I know, Your Honour. I apologise, but we can't engage in the dissection this way. We're not rats. We can't separate the brain from the heart and produce Frankensteins here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I have just a few more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
