utterances.text: Is it correct to say the JNA took away the arms of the Territorial Defence after the parliamentary elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And can we draw the conclusion that Mr. Izetbegovic and other members of the Presidency were not able to prevent these weapons being taken away from the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that the Croats participated in the referendum massively?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that on the second day they supported the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina because Franjo Tudjman had appealed to them and said, Participate in the elections and confirm the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that at the time, but there was only the cardinal or Tudjman who could have taken action at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see 321 on the screen. And while waiting for it you said that after the meeting in Jablanica no one returned to Prozor. Other witnesses deny this to a certain extent. 321, P 00321. While waiting for it to appear, let me ask you the following: Do you know that Daidza was born in 1929. In 1945 he was 16. Towards the end of the 1950s he emigrated to the USA.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I expressed myself erroneously. In Yugoslavia, we refer to these political emigrants in a certain way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You identified them with communists. The Americans thought he was a political emigrant, but the former communist authorities see them in a different way. He returned as an American citizen. 3D 00560. 3D 00560. You'll see a letter from Mr. Alija Izetbegovic to Daidza Zejnil. It says response to the telefax dated the 9th of June, 1992. You should go there together. Zejnil will remain the commander of his unit, or while this -- or, rather, while this operation is ongoing, he must obey Daidza's orders. Daidza shall lead the action and we will deal with everything else when we see each other in Sarajevo. Then it says the 10th June, 1992, is that correct, signed Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that probably is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let's see 3D 00450. 3D 00450. This is a decision we've already seen. Please turn it around. Signed by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, this little letter by -- signed Alija, to what operation does it -- does it refer? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] The operation being prepared for liberating Sarajevo and Igman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please have a look at the first page. What you have just seen was written down on a piece of paper. Let's have a look at item 1. The following Territorial Defences will be established. The Bosnian-Herzegovinian brigade, Kralj Tomislav. King Tomislav was a Croatian King. As brigade commander, we hereby appoint General Mate Sarlija; that's Daidza. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. We don't need the document anymore. This is like playing a game of chess, a rapid game of chess. Ismet Hadziosmanovic, do you know that name?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Recently he wrote a book, and on page 67, I can't tender this. I'll just read out three lines and we'll deal with the book in greater detail later on. He says the following: "Most of the weapons," and this is page 67 of the book, "Most of the weapons came from the Croatian army, and Mate Sarlija, Daidza, personally distributed them, and the Crisis Staff of Croatia for assisting Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina." And then one paragraph further on it says: "As authorised by Gojko Susak, Daidza spoke to Mustafa Hadziosmanovic so that he would be a guarantee that weapons distributed to the Muslims were distributed correctly." And then one line later: "The arms, the weapons, were continually delivered in minor quantities. Daidza delivered a total of 4.500 rifles and a significant amount of ammunition." Are you familiar with anything of this?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. That gentleman was regarded as a traitor in Muslim circles. He handed over the authority in Mostar to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'm not talking about that, Witness. I won't take much of your time.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All people in Mostar write books. I don't know whether you've noticed this. They all speak against everyone else. Everyone is lying. That's how things work.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I think that the Judges and Mr. Scott is listening to this too. Everyone lies.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was talking about the Muslims in Mostar. They write books of 1.500 pages. They all attack everyone. They all attack each other. I'm not referring to Croats. It's terrible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: That's terrible. That's terrible and everyone lies.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: On page 68, the following page, we have a document which we'll show the Judges later. It says -- Daidza wrote to Alija Izetbegovic: "There are 3.000 barrels that I stole from my state, the Republic of Croatia. Let it be a halal for you. It will be forgiven." I have another two questions. Are you familiar with the name Edo Omeragic, a Muslim from Mostar? The second man in your power stations. An electrical engineer from Mostar.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps he had that position, but he wasn't at that level. I know what the hierarchy was -- was like. When Jurkovic appointed officials, well, they were at the top level. That was the case before the war and after the war.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Edo Omeragic was the second in line.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: We'll prove that. Do you know that this man cooperated with the electrical industry in Croatia and managed to maintain the electrical system in Herceg-Bosna and Bosnia-Herzegovina, because without the Elektrodalmacija network it would have been impossible for that network to function?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's probably correct in technical terms. It couldn't have functioned because the network had been disrupted in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that there were discussions between the states about this matter and discussions about the prices?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I can't go back to the power station in Jablanica. It failed to include 150 megawatts in the electrical system and to enable the Cvitovic station to function. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Jablanica had two systems towards Mostar that had been interrupted. They had three systems to Sarajevo. They had also been disrupted. And there was one line to Konjic. So there were these six lines from the power station.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know how much money, time, and effort is necessary to make these power lines function and do you know that we managed to do that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a difficult task.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: One private question. Your father was ill in 1992. He was in Split?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And he recovered?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you pay for his treatment in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] And I thank Your Honours for granting me extra time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I put just one question to this witness we weren't able to prepare because it wasn't contained in earlier statements. Just one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hello, sir. I just have one question on behalf of Mr. Praljak. A minute ago you mentioned that all the writers from Mostar "lied."

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the Muslims, not to the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you perhaps seen a book written by Suad Cupina?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I read that book, I was completely disappointed. The book only consists of lies. It's a total lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, a total lie?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, do you have any re-examination perhaps? I'm saying perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I'd like to do it after the break, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In that case we'll have our 20-minute break, and if the Prosecution could move on rapidly since we have another witness and we have to finish with that witness today. Please be expeditious. It's 20 to 11.00. We'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have the floor, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Idrizovic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: An awful lot of material has been thrown at you, but I only have time to ask you very few questions in follow-up. Could I please ask you to turn again to Exhibit P 00624, either in hard copy or on the screen, whichever is easier. And if I could direct your attention, sir -- if you could find as we discussed earlier and on the cross-examination point 2, agenda item number 2, and then specifically in both the B/C/S and the English version the fifth paragraph. Well, including the one headed "Agenda item 2." It's the fifth paragraph, the paragraph that then begins: "If we wish to create a better environment for more successful defence ..." Do you see that? It's on the bottom of page 6 of the English version, and it's on the fifth numbered page of the B/C/S version. The paragraph starts with the words, sir: "If we wish to create a better environment ..." I may have misspoke. It may have been the fourth paragraph, including the agenda item 2. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On page 5, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "If we wish" -- I have just some language and I have a couple of questions for you. "If we wish to create a better environment for a more successful defence of the municipality, more contacts and cooperation between the OS and the HVO are needed." Now, first of all, in the way that the -- I don't know how it's been interpreted -- I don't know what the B/C/S version is, the Bosnian version is, but "OS," are those the defence forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And then continuing over, or continuing in the same paragraph, skipping a few words, and then it says: "It should be openly said that the Muslim people will not accept three ethnic entities which are currently being imposed." Do you see that language, sir?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that at that time the three entities were, one, the Republika Srpska of the RS; secondly, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; and the third entity being the existing legal state of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission I can consider that to treat Bosnia-Herzegovina as an ethnic whole is quite wrong, or a national entity, and this is what this sentence says in the minutes of the Municipal Assembly Jablanica. There is no dilemma that the two ethnic entities are territorial entities in which three constituent peoples would represent the majority people. I think it is completely unfounded to look at territory outside Bosnia-Herzegovina and Republika Srpska as an ethnic whole, an ethnic entity. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to -- I think the document and -- the witness has spoken and the document speaks for itself. We can argue about it -- we can argue about it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, does that document and including the first part that I read to you, is that consistent with what you've told us about the last three days about your -- reflecting in your personal efforts to maintain continuing cooperation between the HVO and the ABiH as long as you possibly could?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I would like to ask you now about -- you were asked a tremendous number of questions about Konjic and the imbalance of military forces between the Muslim side and the Croat side, at least in terms of soldiers on the ground; that is, infantry. Can you tell the Judges -- in connection with the imbalance of forces, sir, can you tell the Judges from your military assessment, did you consider that the threat to Jablanica came from the direction of Konjic, that the principal threat came from the direction of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I never said that, nor is that possible. Our threat could only have come from -- a threat to us could only have come from the west, which is where it come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in fact you said that among others, you said that the HVO units that attacked the area of Jablanica, including Sovici, Doljani on the 16th and 17th of April, that included HVO units from Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I object to the question. The Defence in the cross-examination never broached the subject of units from Siroki Brijeg. It's a question that the Prosecutor ought to have asked during examination-in-chief. It is not redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's not correct, Your Honour. I'm directly responding to a huge amount of time and material that was spent talking about what was happening in Konjic, and the witness himself tried to give answers about the fact that that was not in fact where the threat came from. And this is legitimate redirect to clarify that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, apart from the HVO units that came from Siroki Brijeg, do you know where any of the other HVO units came for outside -- that came from that were outside the area -- from outside the area of Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the many documents that you all have here, we can see which units they were, and from the documents that the Croatian side provided to the Prosecution I have a list of persons who were killed on the territory of our municipality, Croatian -- and they are HVO documents, SIS documents, or whoever. But the source is Croatian at any rate. If you want me to read out how many soldiers from what municipalities in Western Herzegovina were killed in Jablanica, I can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, we don't have time to do that at the moment, but can you remember the names of any of the other HVO units or the municipalities from which they came outside of Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to remind you that the witness told us that he did not leave Jablanica municipality and that he was not present in Sovici and Doljani and that precisely for that reason we were not granted the right to ask the witness questions about that because there are no sources of information about Sovici and Doljani. So I would like to ask the Prosecution to request those -- to respect those restrictions, because several Defence counsel got up and said that the witness could testify about Sovici and Doljani, but we moved on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, as far as Sovici and Doljani are concerned, there will be other witnesses available, so there's no point in wasting time with this witness; whereas other people will be able to talk about that, address the matter. So move on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I won't belabour it then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, there was also -- it came up in direct examination -- excuse me, in cross-examination that on the morning of approximately the 15th of April when the HVO shelling of Jablanica started that approximately a hundred HVO soldiers that remained -- still remained in Jablanica town were disarmed. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But that figure of 100 was not one I mentioned. I think the figure was 40-odd. You have information in the MUP. It was -- the number was not as high as 100.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us, though, and please assist the Judges as far as you can, when -- is it that these -- I'll use your term -- your number, these 40-odd HVO members, were they disarmed and left at that, or were they arrested and imprisoned?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the attack, I think that the MUP carried out a search of the apartments and houses of military recruits, members of the HVO who remained in Jablanica. Now, what they did with them after that I really can't say. I don't know whether they arrested them or what. I really don't know what happened to them next.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, it was suggested, I think, I don't have the transcript words in front of me at the moment, that these hundred, the number that the Defence uses is approximately a hundred, HVO members were taken into custody, if you were, on that date, on the 15th of April. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. Possibly, but I said I didn't know for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Can I ask you please to look at Exhibit P 00776, which is both in the Prosecution bundle, and I would ask the usher to assist with making it available in e-court, please. Sir, just one or two questions about that. If you can just quickly look at that document long enough to see essentially what it is. And for the record, it's an ABiH order dated the 10th of November, 1992. In the first paragraph it refers to the order that I believe that was referred to during the Praljak cross-examination, making reference to an order signed -- "signed by General Praljak." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've been provided with an order here from Jovan Divjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, correct. And in that first paragraph of that order do you see that it refers to an order by General Praljak?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to an agreement, based on an agreement from a meeting of representatives from the BH army and HVO on the 31st of October. So this is after the fall of Prozor when attempts were being made to influence the situation and to place the territory under control, some kind of control, because the situation was very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Idrizovic. And does this document in fact reflect that the ABiH command issued an order to engage for there to be mixed military check-points and patrols? That is, it was not only Mr. Praljak but the ABiH side issued a similar order; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Well, I said that they did this on the basis of a joint agreement, and then both sides issued orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I would like you to -- just one or two more questions or two topics. If I could ask you to look quickly at -- I think it was Defence Exhibit -- well, in this case it was marked as Defence Exhibit 3D 00561. It's a presidential transcript from the 27th of March, 1993. And if I could direct, please, for the English readers it will be on page -- if you look at the L numbers, I'm referring to page -- well, let's start with the same -- from one of the earlier reference by counsel, L0068585. In the B/C/S version, sir, I think it will be approximately -- well, I've changed my own reference. I apologise, sir. I've changed my own reference. But for the sake of speed, Your Honours, let me go straight to the English reference on page L0068588. And, Mr. Idrizovic, in the Bosnian version page -- the ERN page 01322423.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Usher, I think he may need some assistance on this. It was a Praljak exhibit, 3D 00561. And for the witness specifically, B/C/S ERN page 01322423.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, about the middle of that page -- well, let me double-check the B/C/S version again. You'll see on that page there's a statement -- there's a statement attributed to the president which we can see from the transcript is President Tudjman. Does -- do you see the words where it says -- Tudjman says: "The reasons lie in the fact that the HVO is forcibly establishing parallel authorities." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, is that in fact consistent with what you saw happening on the ground during 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think the document speaks for itself, and if you extract the sentence it and quote it alone, then you have extracted it from its context, because one must have a look at what came before and what came afterwards. But my objection is that the document speaks for itself, and there's absolutely no need for the witness to expound on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, exactly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges will consider the matter. Ask the question directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. My only comment very briefly in response to Mr. Kovacic is that is exactly my reason for raising it, is to show that in the same passage of the transcript raised by Defence counsel there's this other statement by President Tudjman which certainly should be considered indeed in context.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Finally, sir, if I can show you in connection with the museum in Jablanica, which was again the subject of extensive questioning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Counsel. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, but the text read out I can see on the screen. So if Mr. Scott takes a look at that, it is a quotation from the statement of another individual, and if you look at what the president says two paragraphs above, you'll see that he's referring to what Ambassador Ilic said and not what President Tudjman said. I can see it on my screen in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to argue about it now. If you look -- I think everyone -- English readers on page L0068588. I'll let the document indeed speak for itself and what President Tudjman says.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in connection with the museum in Jablanica which you were extensively questioned about, let me ask you, please, to be shown Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Prlic. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] Thank you. Just one technical intervention. In the transcript the words refer to a document which was introduced by Mr. Praljak with the signatures of seven individuals from Konjic, and the person who is saying this, Izetbegovic, says it's this document. So that's the document he's referring to. And later on they go on to quote words from the document. So this is a technical intervention and comment, to say that you cannot analyse a document of this kind in that way. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you, Mr. Idrizovic, to please look at Exhibit P 06528. And this is not in a bundle because it's only arisen during the course of the cross -- or -- yes, the cross-examination. So if I could please have the assistance of the usher in e-court. Exhibit P 06528. If you can have that and if we can -- turning your attention, sir if you can find this is an ECMM report dated the 8th of November, 1993, and if I can ask you to look at number -- item number 5, page 2 of both the B/C/S and the English version in e-court. Item 5. "M1 visited the refugee and POW camp in the Jablanica museum where conditions were described as appalling. Over 600 refugees (Muslim and Croat) are accommodated in the building in addition to 41 Croat prisoners in five cells. There is urgent need for supplies, in particular clothing." Now, sir, is that consistent with what you've told the Chamber as observed by international representatives, that both Croats and Muslims were housed at the museum in unfortunately difficult conditions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Counsel. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise, but I think that during the cross-examination the witness said that he might have visited the museum once after the period that those prisoners of war were there. So we should establish whether that was on the 8th of November, 1993, or before -- several months before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's another thing, Your Honour. When the witness spoke about the museum, unless I am very much mistaken, he referred to a later period, I think he mentioned March 1993, whereas this is November 1992 -- 1993. So obviously it is not the same period of time and the situation certainly changed in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, there were questions throughout 1993 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, this document refers to November and apparently there were refugees in November with several detainees in their cells. Yesterday the witness was asked about March, so bear that in mind when you ask him the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. I think -- I appreciate that. But just today there were questions about what happened later in the fall of 1993 in the museum. And counsel repeatedly -- repeated Defence teams spent extensive time talking about the museum and either saying directly or implying criticism and -- of this particular witness, and I think it's appropriate redirect to give him the chance to clarify it. And in response to the reports that are available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the only question after the event in Sovici and Doljani which relates to the later period was whether the museum, possibly in September, was planned to become an Islamic centre. Mr. Scott refers to my questions, but they had nothing to do with whether at that point in time there were detainees or refugees there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, ask your question to clarify this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Simply, Your Honour, if I can -- it's obvious the Defence does not want me to conduct this redirect, but if I can have -- if I can ask two additional questions, I'll be finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you can please look at P 06448.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're not going to ask any more questions about the museum?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Your Honour, but I'm referring now to an exhibit, the next exhibit, which is P 06448.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. I'm going ask the witness a question. In the document we have on our screens, it seems that there were 600 refugees in November who were put up in the museum. Do you remember that? Can you confirm that, the observation made by somebody else who was an international observer? Can you confirm that yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that in a previous statement of mine I said that the situation generally speaking and especially in the museum was very difficult. Ten thousand refugees in November were there -- were -- came in. Now, the refugees who were put up in the museum were the last refugees to arrive in Jablanica. This is not a nice thing to say, but all the refugees were given better accommodation, if I can put it that way, than the last ones coming in, both Croats and Muslims. Now, the reports are correct, and I had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document shows that there were 600 refugees, and in brackets it says "Muslims and Croats."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The next document I've been informed is under seal, so if we could not be broadcast for the moment. There is nothing about it that will be identified but just that it not be broadcast outside the courtroom, the document itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But if I could refer you to Exhibit, sir, P 06448, and again in e-court, please. If I can ask you to look at again item number 5, humanitarian. And while we're doing this, this is again an ECMM report dated the 5th of November, 1993. And when you see, sir, the language again at page 2 of both the English and the B/C/S version, it says, among other things: "But all have free access to the town." Now, you've said a couple of times and during both direct and cross-examination, I think, and I want to ask you again to clarify: Throughout this time period, as far as you know, were both the Muslims and the Croat refugees housed at the museum given, quote, as in this document, "free access to the town"?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And finally, sir, if I can refer you to the next document which is - and that's my last question, Your Honour - Exhibit P 05422. P 05422 in e-court, please. You have that, sir. The numbering starts -- the lettering starts again, but if you go to approximately the second page in both the English and the Bosnian version and the second heading A. There's an earlier A and then there's a second series of numbers starting with A, paragraphs starting with A. Referring to a meeting with Kresimir Zubak from the HV -- the vice-president of the HVO. Do you see this language, sir: "A, he said he would be very pleased to see an ECMM team up in Jablanica. There were 640 Croats in Jablanica which included 200 from Doljani who were living in the museum in the town." In B/C/S I'm told it's on page 3. "They were not being treated badly by the Muslims but conditions were very bad in the museum." Again, sir, is that consistent with the facts and information as you saw or were aware of at that time?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Idrizovic, once again I thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that's all my questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the Chamber would also like to thank you for having come in to testify. You have spent almost a week here in court, so we'd like to express our gratitude to you for that and wish you bon voyage back home. I'm going to ask Madam Usher to escort you out of the courtroom now, and also ask the registrar to lower the blinds so that we can have the next witness shown in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're now going to have witnesses who are going to testify about Sovici and Doljani, and I'd like to remind everyone that the Chamber has made a ruling on adjudicated facts with Naletilic and judicial notice. We have had judicial notice of this, and they should be considered as being true. Now, if the Defence would like to challenge that, they can do so on the basis of irrefutable documents. Otherwise, those facts, as far as the Chamber is concerned, are presumed to be true. By way of an example for everybody to be able to understand what I'm saying, fact 54, and I'd like to quote from the Judgement, and it refers to the mid -- that there was an open conflict between the BiH and HVO. As far as we're concerned, that has already been established unless you are able to show otherwise. 26 -- paragraph 26, attacks on villages with an HVO offensive destined to gain control of Jablanica. So another Trial Chamber said that the HVO was engaged in an offensive. If you wish to prove the contrary, you must show it based on valid documents. I'm telling you this in order to gain time. We're now going to have the witness shown in. There are protective measures put in place. Mr. Scott, would you like to explain why.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Previously. Mr. Poryvaev will actually be taking the witness, but I did want to address the procedural matters first. First of all, Your Honour, for the record and in light of what the President just said, the Prosecution has indeed limited the evidence that it will present in court based upon the existence of the adjudicated facts. In our view, and the Chamber may ultimately agree or disagree with us, of course, but I do want to say for the record in our view we are calling a very -- a very limited amount of courtroom evidence concerning Sovici and Doljani. It will be only probably about a week of witnesses because we assumed the Court would want to have some viva voce evidence, and that the -- and that the Defence likewise would want to have some opportunity to cross-examine. But indeed in reliance on the fact that there are the adjudicated facts the Prosecution is only presenting a very limited case. As to the witness, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, the counsel is right. The witness statement, record, was redacted because it was part of supporting material, and it was disclosed to the Defence at that particular period of time, which was justified by the conditions of providing the Defence with the supporting material. But nothing special had been redacted which would be prejudicial to the Defence, just some whereabouts information and whereabouts. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really don't want to waste any time. I agree with what my colleague has said. Yes, according to the practice of this Court, when the supporting material is provided, some of the material was redacted. We didn't object. That's how it was. But when this witness was announced, it was necessary to provide us with a full statement. Not for the traditional reasons, but also because this statement is now being tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, you have the redacted version. Could you give me the version so that I can compare it to the full version. I see that the three redacted paragraphs and these paragraphs in fact enable us to identify the witness. So there is nothing that would be prejudicial to the Defence. Here you are. I'll give you the document back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, but I hope that the statement that will be tendered into evidence will at least be the complete version of the document, that it will be a statement that hasn't been redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, of course. We have prepared unredacted version of the statement, and we intend to tender it into evidence in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but this version will be under seal since there will be paragraphs that enable one to identify the witness. Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness BZ. I've got some questions to you relevant to your witness statement given at some time to the investigators of the International Tribunal. Did you in fact give any statement to any investigator of the International Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: That statement was given on the 3rd of May, 1997; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: At the time when you were giving your witness statement, did you answer the questions of the investigator truthfully?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you answer the questions freely, that is, without any coercion?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And at the end of the interview, were you given an opportunity of reading your statement in your native language through an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like the witness to be provided with his witness statements both in English and in B/C/S version. I don't think that they should be placed on the ELMO, because he attached his signature in such a way that his identity will be easily revealed if it's seen in public.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, I would like you to take a look at both versions of this statement now, in English and B/C/S version. Could you tell us what version was signed by you, English or B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: When you came to The Hague some days ago, you were given an opportunity of re-reading your statements both in English and B/C/S version, right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: When you were reviewing your witness statement in B/C/S version, did you notice anything that should be changed, deleted, or amended now?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you confirm your witness statement given on the 5th of May, 1997?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, if it were your testimony today, if you were asked by myself the whole range of questions touched upon in your witness statement, would it be your testimony now?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I'd provide you with a broader version.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Why do you think so? Do you recall any facts you --

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I'd go into greater detail, provide you with more explanations in relation to certain things.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: With the Trial Chamber's leave, maybe I'll ask you some questions just to clarify some allegations in your witness statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender the witness statement given by this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Poryvaev.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Poryvaev, we've issued very specific instructions. The Prosecution should provide a very brief summary of the contents of his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour. The witness was living in Sovici, and at some point, he was involved in the defence of Sovici area when the HVO launched the attack on Sovici on the 17th of April, 1993. Among other group of villagers, he had to surrender himself to HVO authorities and was taken to -- to the Ljubuski prison where he spent for some -- for some period of time and then transferred to Heliodrom where he was involved in forced labour and on the 10th of August was wounded. The witness was released from Heliodrom in March 1994. So, Your Honour, I would like to tender --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: -- this statement as our Exhibit number 9727 under seal. With your leave, Your Honour, I would like to clarify some allegations and the witness statement record which in my point of view needs some clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours. Your Honours, on a number of occasions we already discussed how this new rule should be applied, and I believe we've already decided that we can't have it both ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The only clarifications that are allowed consist in showing the witness documents that relate to the relevant paragraphs. Otherwise, this procedure is completely useless.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: That's what I intend to do, Your Honour. Perhaps my learned colleague misunderstood me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then go ahead with the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Anyway, all my questions will be related to the documents I intend to tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: So, Witness, you arrived in Ljubuski on the 19th of April, 1993; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And according to your statement on page 4, you stayed there for about two months or a month and a half, and then you were transferred to Heliodrom; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: On when you came to Heliodrom, you saw some people from Jablanica who had been transferred to Heliodrom before; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see how this question relates to the documents that we have. We have three photographs here, and we have one document from the 4th Battalion in Posusje. Please do respect the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I do respect the rules, my learned colleague, and my questions are related to Exhibit 2535, which I would like to be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That's how one should have proceeded. You should have said you stayed in Ljubuski for two months. I will now show you document 2535. Have a look at the document. Can you see your name on it, and he'd say yes and then we'd move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We haven't received that document for this witness. I don't think any of the Defence teams has this document. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] This document isn't even in our chart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you provide the Defence with this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, all the documents were provided to the Defence, and they were in our chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps it would be best if I gave you my bundle of documents, which is in good order, and you'll see that we don't have that document. We have three documents or, rather, four mentioned by my colleague. And as my colleagues say, this document isn't included in either of the two charts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I've got the document with -- I've got the bundle with 2535, and I see that in the list of exhibits this document is included. It should be included in the -- in the 95 ter list. I assume that's the case. Yes, Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This document that we can see on the screen was intended for another witness, as far as I know, not for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's wrong. We provided the Trial Chamber, the Defence team with the chart of all our statements, all our documents that stand for Jablanica witnesses, including this one. So we were not supposed to make any special binder for this witness. Once he's included in the list of witnesses, he is not a new witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I understand the problem. As a rule, the instructions should have been clear. If a witness appears, 92 ter witness or viva voce witness, the Prosecution has to provide the Defence with a list of exhibits. That's what you do. And I believe that in fact you only provided the Defence with four documents, and now at the very last minute the Defence notices that there are more than four documents. We have a mystery. Why did you only refer to four documents originally, whereas there are about 10 of them? Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apology to my colleague for intervening, but I think there is a misunderstanding, Your Honour. In the set of materials that were sent out to the Defence on the 20th of October, all the charts were attached I think as one document, but there are headings that break down per witness. I'm looking at it on our screen right now in terms of the Prosecution record, and the document I'm looking at in fact lists the four exhibits, the exact exhibits that Mr. Poryvaev has mentioned. So I think it's simply a question -- I think there's been some confusion. The list was indeed sent out to the Defence and it's included in what was sent on the 20th of October is what our information shows. Now, if for some reason there was some sort of mistake, then obviously it needs to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave. There obviously has been a mistake, and I don't want to add anything else to my what my colleagues have already said. It's quite obvious that we received a chart for this witness and with the help of the usher I can show it to you, and the chart only refers to four documents. If the Prosecution believes that all the exhibits that concern one part of the indictment are exhibits that we should always have on us for each and every witness, in that case it's necessary to inform us in advance. We have prepared our cross-examination on the basis of the documents referred to in this chart. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, on the 20th of October was there 9726, 2131, 2535, and 9070? Were all these exhibits included on the 20th of October? If that's the case, show me the documents so I can check this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The legal officer has told me certainly, but not in connection with the right witness. On the 20th of October, you must have provided an entire list of exhibits without specifically referring to this witness and that's how the mistake was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour I think is correct. In talking with Mr. Poryvaev and the case manager, what appears to have happened is and I would be -- we confess to an error, apparent error that was made. When the original list was sent, it did in fact only include the -- on the 16th of -- excuse me, on the 20th of October, it did include as to this witness only four, but all the total exhibits that would be used in connection with Sovici and Doljani were all part of a master list, if you will. But it appears that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We've understood the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It appears now that in fairness to Mr. Poryvaev in preparing for the witness that other documents that are on the master list but were not included in that subset have been added, and counsel -- with that clarification, I accept that counsel are correct on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should nonetheless like to highlight a detail that is being forgotten here. Of course mistakes can always happen. That's no problem. I accept what my learned colleague has just said. The documents were mixed up. It is evident that we were warned which documents would be used along with this witness, and we were given that caution in two ways. Our attention was drawn to that on the basis of the review of documents that we received together with other documents for other witnesses, and then there was a large document specifying each individual witness. So we're speaking about one witness here, who has a name, and the documents that the Prosecution plans to tender and present through him. Bearing in mind that it is 95 ter procedure, we have to prepare for it. We go to our own database on the basis of the information provided us from the Prosecution, which was in this case four documents. Now, our own preparation, within our own preparation we have to take a look at another chart or, rather, two charts, and they are the ones from the 4th of September this year when a final ruling was received from the Court of the 30th of November last year, because that chart, according to the definition given not in the Trial Chamber's ruling is of tantamount importance, and I think that that particular chart, or master chart, controls the situation. I don't want to repeat the purpose for which you rendered your ruling to have these charts compiled, and I'd like to say that for this particular witness there were only two documents that were envisaged. Just two documents with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to end the discussion. We accept that the documents which are in this file be presented to the witness, but in future pay greater attention to those matters, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Again, it was our error and we accept that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: So I would like witness to be shown Exhibit 2535.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to move into private session because if there are any names that appear, that would be prudent.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a witness will be appearing on Monday, according to plan, and this witness shouldn't take up the entire day, we could then deal with the comments that the parties would like to make with regard to protective measures. We are adjourning a few minutes late, but I invite you all to turn for the hearing at 2.15 on Monday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
